findings.title: TfL website 'hacked' affecting hundreds of thousands of Oyster photocard users
findings.summary_md: Metro reported on 18 November that Transport for London had taken its Oyster photocard website offline after noticing suspicious activity on 16 November. TfL said about 265,000 photocard customers might have had account details exposed, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth and security questions and answers. The article says all photocard customers were advised to change their passwords and security questions and answers, and that TfL had found no evidence at that point of the data being used.

findings.title: Oyster photocard holders' personal data accessed in TfL breach
findings.summary_md: The BBC reported that TfL had notified the Information Commissioner's Office after suspicious activity on the photocard website, and quoted director of technology strategy and revenue Shashi Verma saying about 265,000 customers may have had account details compromised. TfL said the breach was detected on Monday morning when some customers received unexpected emails asking them to validate accounts, and that the system was shut down immediately. TfL said no photos, passwords, bank or payment card details, journey information, or names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were compromised.

findings.title: TfL issues apology to Oyster card customers over data breach after 'suspicious activity' detected
findings.summary_md: The Independent published the notification TfL sent to affected customers, which said suspicious activity on 16 November led to unauthorised access to personal information in web accounts despite action to limit access and take the photocard system offline. It reported that names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth and security questions and answers were affected, while passwords, bank and payment card details, journey histories and Zip Oyster children's names and birth dates were not. The potentially affected account types listed were Zip Oyster cards for ages 5-10, 11-15 and 16+, 18+ Student, 18-25 Care Leaver, 60+ London, Apprentice and Veterans photocards; travel and ticket-machine top-ups continued while online access was disabled.

findings.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
findings.summary_md: The Register reported that TfL had not disclosed how the perpetrators entered its systems and had found no evidence that the compromised data had been used. It noted that holders of Zip Oyster cards, students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans and Londoners aged 60 and over were among those potentially affected, and that TfL would ask all photocard customers to change passwords and security questions and answers. The article compared this with the September 2024 TfL attack, when more than 7 million customers were notified and about 5,000 were contacted because bank details might have been accessed; two teenagers were later charged and authorities linked that attack to Scattered Spider, with no evidence at publication that the incidents were related.

findings.title: TfL reports second photocard breach to ICO nine months after London Assembly cyber review
findings.summary_md: Info-Gov.uk reported that TfL had notified the ICO and was asking photocard customers to change passwords, security questions and answers, and to change passwords on other services using the same information. It said the photocard website remained offline, renewals and journey-history queries would go through Customer Services on 0343 222 1234, and Freedom Pass applications were unaffected because London Councils handles them. The article noted TfL's 2024 breach prompted more than 7.1 million customer notifications, about 5,000 heightened-risk contacts and a February 2025 ICO decision that formal regulatory action was not proportionate.
